text: The bread is out of the oven and the kitchen window has fogged over from the inside. I turn the radio down until it is mostly murmur and lean against the counter with the loaf cooling beside me. There is nowhere I need to be for the rest of the evening.

The dog has put his head on my foot and gone to sleep, and I am not going to move it. Down the street the neighbors' sprinkler ticks back and forth across their lawn. I sip what is left of my iced tea and watch the light go out of the sky.

The last sock has found its match and the stacks of laundry sit square on the bed. Late sun comes across the quilt and lands on my hands. I smooth the top towel once more than it needs and leave the pile where it is.

My son is asleep in the back seat with sand still on his legs and the beach towel wadded under his cheek. I drive the slow way home with the windows down two inches. Every few minutes I check the mirror just to see him breathing.

I have watered the whole garden and the tomato vines hang heavy against their stakes. The soil under my fingernails will take a scrub brush to get out. I sit on the overturned bucket and let the hose drip onto my boots.

The Sunday paper is spread across the table in sections and my second cup of coffee is still hot. The calendar on the fridge shows nothing until Tuesday. I fold the crossword back and settle deeper into the chair.

The hallway is painted and the rollers are soaking in the sink. I stand at one end and look down the length of it with the overhead light on. The color came out exactly the way it looked on the little card.

An hour has gone by on the phone with my oldest friend and I have refilled the kettle twice. Her voice sounds the same as it did when we were nineteen. I pull my feet up under me on the couch and let her finish the story.

Rain runs down the glass and the cat has arranged herself along the windowsill with her tail over her nose. My book is open on my knee at a page I have read twice without minding. The radiator ticks and settles.

The sauce tastes the way it did in my grandmother's kitchen, which has never happened before. I stand over the pot with the wooden spoon and take one more taste to be sure. Then I turn the flame down low and set the table for two.

The grocery bags cut a little into my fingers on the walk home, and from the corner I can see our apartment lights already on. Somebody is moving around in the kitchen. I shift the bags to one hand and dig for my keys without hurrying.

My legs are still humming from the ride and my shoes are off on the front step beside me. The bike leans against the railing with mud dried on its frame. I drink the whole bottle of water in one long pull and sit a while longer.

The first fire of the season is going in the woodstove and the split logs are stacked to the window ledge. I hold my palms out toward the glass door until they are almost too warm. The house smells like smoke and oranges.

She falls asleep in the middle of the page about the bear, her hand still on the picture. I keep reading in a whisper for another minute anyway. When I close the book I leave the lamp on and sit on the edge of the bed.

The fridge is full for the first time in two weeks, with the milk in the door and the vegetables washed and in their drawer. I stand with the door open longer than I should, just looking. Then I close it and wipe the handle with my sleeve.

The bedroom door has squeaked for three years and now it swings shut without a sound. I open it and close it twice more to be sure. The little can of oil goes back under the sink with its cap on tight.

I lean in the kitchen doorway and watch him chop onions with the knife I sharpened last weekend. He hums something I half recognize and does not know I am there yet. The pan is already warming on the back burner.
My feet hang off the end of the dock into water that is colder than the air. The boat knocks softly against its bumpers behind me. A dragonfly lands on my knee, considers it, and goes.

The monthly numbers come out with a little room to spare, which they have not done since spring. I write the total at the bottom of the page and underline it once. The pen goes back in the mug and I stretch my arms over my head.

I press the last tulip bulb into the cold ground and pat the soil over it with the flat of my hand. There are forty of them under here now, pointed end up, waiting for April. I wipe my hands on my jeans and look at the empty bed.

The rows add up under my needles while the television murmurs about weather somewhere else. The scarf is long enough now to reach my knees when I hold it up. I count the stitches once more and keep going.

Rain streaks the coffee shop window and steam rises off the cup in front of me. I have three clues left in the crossword and no plans for the afternoon. The woman at the next table laughs at something in her book.
The hammock holds me between two trunks and the leaves above shift light across my face. Somewhere a lawnmower starts and stops. I let one arm hang down until my fingertips brush the grass.

Half the sky is done, a thousand pieces of nearly the same blue, and the kitchen table has been covered for a week. I find the one with the wisp of cloud and press it in. My tea has gone cold and I drink it anyway.

The sheets are fresh from the line and I am clean from the shower, and it is not even nine o'clock. I slide in and pull the blanket up to my chin. The window is open a crack and the crickets are at it.
We walk the loop after dinner as the porch lights come on one by one along the block. My hand is in her coat pocket with hers. Neither of us says much and neither of us needs to.

The kids have pulled every cushion off the couch and built something with a tunnel and two rooms. I sit on the bare frame with my coffee and watch them negotiate the roof. Nobody has asked me for anything in twenty minutes.

The chain is oiled and the brakes grab clean and I take the bike once around the block to be sure. It shifts through every gear without a click. I roll it back into the garage and hang it on its hooks.

My mother and I shell peas on the back step with the colander between us. Her thumbnail splits each pod the same way it always has. The pile of empty shells grows beside her slipper and the pods ping into the bowl.

The envelope is addressed in my old teacher's handwriting, the same slant as on my report cards. I read the letter twice standing in the hall and then once more sitting down. I prop it against the sugar bowl where I will see it tomorrow.
Rain hammers the tin roof of the cabin and the cards are dealt for another hand. The woodstove has the room warm enough for socks and no shoes. My brother shuffles badly and nobody points it out.

The dog comes home from the groomer smelling of something floral and sits in the patch of sun on the kitchen floor. I sit down next to her with my back against the cabinet. We stay there until the sun moves.
The bakery bag is warm against my chest on the walk back and the whole street smells of it. I tear off the end of one roll before I reach the corner. Saturday has barely started.
The clay finally centers on the wheel after six weeks of wobbling, and a bowl rises between my hands almost on its own. I slow the wheel and let it spin to a stop. My forearms are gray to the elbow.
Nothing has taken the bait since dawn and the thermos is half empty. Mist lifts off the pond in slow sheets. I recast toward the reeds because the motion is reason enough.

Everyone is at the table at once, plates going around, someone laughing in the next room over a photo. I pass the potatoes to my left and take the bread from my right. The chair creaks under me the way it has for years.
The tank is clean and the fish are circling the fresh water in slow figure eights. I dry my arms and sit on the floor with my chin on the edge of the stand. The filter hums back up to speed.
Smoke from the grill drifts over the lawn chairs and a ballgame plays from a radio on the porch rail. I turn the corn and let the lid drop. Somebody hands me a cold can without my asking.

Fields slide past the train window in long green bands and my sandwich is still wrapped in foil on the tray. I have a window seat and three hours to go. I unwrap one corner and watch a barn come and go.
The button is back on the coat, the thread knotted twice and snipped. I try it through the buttonhole and it holds. The needle goes back into the little tomato cushion with the others.
The ladder is steady against the apple tree and the bucket at my hip is filling faster than I expected. I twist each one until the stem gives. Below me my daughter is eating more than she is picking.
The watercolor bleeds exactly where I let it, the wash of sky running down into the paper. I rinse the brush and lean back from the balcony table. The afternoon has gotten away from me and I let it.
The walk is shoveled and the bath is as hot as I can stand it. I sink down until the water closes over my shoulders. Through the little window I can see it has started snowing again.

Snow is coming down under the streetlight in the kind of flakes that take their time. I watch from the kitchen with the lights off and a mug in both hands. The plow has not come yet and the street is one smooth white sheet.
The campfire has burned down to the stage where the marshmallows go on, and three small faces lean in toward the coals. I hold my stick low and turn it slowly. Sparks go up and out over the lake.

The guests are gone and the dishwasher is humming through its first cycle. I wipe down the counters in long slow passes and put the last glass in the cabinet. The house holds the sound of the evening a little while longer.

The last box is unpacked and flattened and the books are on their shelves in roughly the right order. I sit on the floor in the middle of the room with my back against the couch. Out the new window there is a tree I had not noticed.
The barber lays the hot towel over my face and the shop goes dim and muffled. Scissors click somewhere to my left. I let my shoulders drop against the chair and stop keeping track of time.
Bubbles rise through the pancake batter and I wait for the edges to go dry before I flip. The kids are still in pajamas arguing about syrup. The stack on the plate is getting tall enough to lean.
I lie on the grass with my hands behind my head while my nephew names the clouds. That one is a dog, that one is also a dog. The ground is warm through my shirt.

The dogs run wide loops across the wet grass of the park and come back muddy to the shins. I stand with the other owners holding a leash I do not need yet. The coffee in my cup is the first of the day.

My father holds the board while I drive the nails, the way he used to hold it for his father. The fence line straightens post by post down the field. My pocket is heavy with the nails we have not used.
I close the cover of the novel and keep my hand flat on it for a moment. Eight hundred pages and the ending landed where it should. The couch cushion has my shape pressed into it.

The peach from the market stall is so ripe the juice runs down my wrist before I can catch it. I eat it standing in the shade of the awning. The farmer hands me a napkin and does not charge me for the second one.

My niece tosses bread to the ducks in handfuls too big for them and the ducks do not mind. I hold the back of her jacket so she does not follow them in. The pond is flat and the morning is going nowhere fast.

Everyone has left the office and my desk is cleared down to the lamp and one folder. The building ticks as it cools. I finish the last line of the report and sit for a minute before I reach for my coat.
